questions.explain: $v_2 = -\tfrac12 v_1$, so the vectors are dependent ($\det[v_1\ v_2] = 0$, rank 1). Every combination $c_1v_1 + c_2v_2$ is a multiple of $v_1$: a single line. Two non-zero vectors do not automatically give the plane.

questions.q: Why does `np.linalg.matrix_rank` compare singular values with a tolerance instead of testing whether the determinant is exactly 0?
options: Because the determinant only exists for 3×3 matrices
Because floating-point rounding makes truly dependent vectors give tiny non-zero values, so 'zero' must mean 'below a tolerance'
Because the tolerance makes the rank larger for every matrix
Because singular values are always integers
questions.explain: With $v_1=(0.1,0.7)$ and $v_2=3v_1$ the computed determinant is about $-5.6\times10^{-17}$, not 0. matrix_rank counts $\sigma_i > \text{tol}$ (default $\sigma_{\max}\cdot\max(m,n)\cdot\varepsilon$), which treats rounding dust as zero.

questions.q: A $3\times 3$ matrix $A$ has rank 2. What is the dimension of its null space $\{x : Ax = 0\}$?
questions.explain: Rank–nullity: rank + nullity = number of columns, so nullity $= 3 - 2 = 1$: a whole line of inputs is crushed to 0.

questions.q: $v_1, v_2$ are independent and $B = [v_1\ v_2]$. How do you find the coordinates $c$ of a point $w$ in the basis $\{v_1, v_2\}$?
options: Coordinates are not unique for a basis
questions.explain: $w = c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 = Bc$, so $c$ solves $Bc = w$; independence makes $B$ invertible and the coordinates unique. Applying $B$ goes the other way (from new coordinates back to standard ones).
